My first birth was textbook...28 hours of labour, most of which wasn't too bad; vaginal delivery; no medication other than a shot of demerol which didn't make it hurt less and instead just made me fall asleep. My second birth was an emergency c-section at 33 weeks. My water broke at 31 weeks and I spent two weeks in the hospital leaking amniotic fluid and bleeding fairly heavily. I went into labour twice and they stopped it twice. The third time I went into labour it didn't stop, but it also didn't progress; the contractions got stronger and closer together but I wasn't dilating and my daughter's heart rate slowed down alarmingly through the contractions. It was very painful; they didn't give me pain meds because preemies can be born very quickly and they were worried that medication may make her APGAR score lower. They ended up doing a c-section around 4 a.m. and it was such a relief after such a difficult labour. I had a spinal and they bungled it up, resulting in losing a bit of spinal fluid and then having a four-day migraine. My feet and calves swelled up terribly after the surgery; no idea why but it was gross. lol Baby girl did just fine and is now a sassy 12-year-old. My c-section scar looks badass. My opinion on c-sections is that they can literally save lives...my daughter would be dead and I probably would be too. If you need one, have one and don't regret it. If you don't need one, though, don't get one; it's major surgery, and the recovery can be really rough. If you can deliver vaginally, do it.

Third birth was a stillbirth. I was ten days out from my due date when I noticed my baby hadn't kicked in a while, which was unusual for her. Long story short, an ultrasound revealed that her heart had stopped and she was gone. I hadn't started labour on my own yet and they decided to induce me. I begged my doctor to do another c-section because I couldn't face the thought of a long labour with a dead baby at the end of it, but she encouraged me to try in case we ever decided to have another baby down the road. Two c-sections means my odds of ever having a successful VBAC would be slim to none. So I opted to try for a VBAC. They gave me an epidural so I wouldn't feel the pain. It worked wonderfully; I felt nothing. That was a mercy because holy crap, the contractions you get from being induced are unbelievably strong. Even with no pain I couldn't catch my breath through the strongest contractions. It was by far my fastest, easiest labour and recovery. But it's still hard to think about that day, even ten years later. The deafening silence in that room as she was born still haunts me.

Anyway. So yeah. Epidurals are not without risk but they work well. Same with c-sections. You need to do your research so you know what you're getting into in case things go sideways on you. You also need to talk to your doctor about all this stuff because knowing that you're on the same page as the person who will help you deliver your baby is important, and also because hearing reassurance from a medical professional is helpful. Don't be scared! It's not easy bringing a baby into the world, but it is what our bodies are designed to handle, and you will be surrounded by people whose job it is to help you. The odds are absolutely in your favour here. :) While you wait, eat well and get as much exercise as you safely can.

I’ve had multiple surgeries over the years (mostly related to my back; I have degenerative disc disease), and I do NOT recover quickly. My first birth was in a hospital in Boston. I wanted a natural birth, but after 19 hours of labor with a posterior baby, I caved and got an epidural. It was what I needed at the time. My body needed to relax, and I was so exhausted and delirious with pain. My husband basically told me I had to get an epi, and in hindsight, he was right. If I tried to soldier on without pain relief, I would have been to exhausted to push, and I probably would have had to have surgery. My son was 9lb3oz, and as I said, posterior. The epi completely numbed me from the waist down, and I couldn’t feel anything. I had a second degree tear, and I won’t lie, it was horribly painful. I had a very difficult recovery, and I almost died of a uterine infection when my son was 12 days old. My husband got me to the ER with maybe an hour to spare (according to the on call OB at the hospital). That was a very scary, traumatic experience, and while my fear wasn’t exactly rational, I became terrified of hospitals.

Second baby: a daughter, had a water birth at a freestanding birth center attended by midwives. Also a 9lb baby, but she wasn’t posterior. No pain meds, but since she was in the correct position, this birth was a cakewalk compared to my last! Very easy recovery, no tearing.

Third baby: another daughter, this time in a hospital. We had moved to a new area, and the Homebirth midwives there didn’t have good reputations. However, I did see a fantastic group of midwives who delivered at a hospital that was very supportive of natural births. Unfortunately my baby girl was posterior, and the back labor was killing me. I got an epidural, but this one was SO much better than my first. I wasn’t completely numb, and I could still feel the contractions and the urge to push. No tearing, and I was up and walking around 2 hours post birth. Very easy recovery.

Fourth baby: same hospital, same group of midwives, I was induced for medical reasons, but I had a natural, med free birth. My son was in the correct position, so again, labor was a breeze! He literally flew out after two pushes, and my midwife had to lunge towards the bed to catch him. 😂

So for me, at least, baby being in the correct position made a world of difference. Of course labor will be painful (it’s called labor for a reason!), but other than my posterior babies, I never felt like labor was ZOMG THE WORST PAIN I’VE EVER FELT IN MY LYFE!!! For me, the worst pain of my life was the gallstone attacks before I had my gallbladder removed. I wouldn’t wish that on my worst enemy.
